prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, narrative and the essay through a sustained encounter with antiquity, and that dissolves the boundaries between genres with formal daring, intellectual depth and emotional force

statement.case_for: After weighing my colleagues' openings, I still place Carson first on the common criteria. Her voice is unmistakable. Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon myth as a verse novel, and Nox makes elegy into a physical, archival object. Both are formal achievements that depend on the material and linguistic choices of the work itself, not on novelty. The intellectual depth comes from long engagement with Greek and Latin literature, so the invention rests on scholarship and feeling together. The work runs through poetry, essay, drama and verse-novel across several decades, and the method has kept moving. It is written in English, so the question of translation does not weaken the linguistic judgment, as it does for Romanian, Arabic and Chinese candidates. A citation naming renewal of lyric and narrative through dialogue with antiquity is coherent for a single writer and does not depend on one title.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is that Carson's reputation may rest on a few landmark books, and I cannot verify from the supplied evidence that quality holds across the whole corpus. Much of the oeuvre is deliberately occasional, fragmentary or object-like. Her translations and scholarly work are hard to weigh against her original creation in a Literature award, and a citation that is too broad could blur that line. Cărtărescu's large, sustained architecture and Robinson's compact, consistent fiction both make a strong claim to sustained quality. I hold this preference with real uncertainty.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for a recognizable visionary voice and a large imaginative architecture across poetry and prose. She ranks Carson second and asks whether the hybrid forms add up to sustained quality over the whole corpus, with unevenness hard to judge.
responses.response: I take the unevenness question seriously and cannot dismiss it. Where I differ is on what the sustained quality is. In Carson it lies in a method that returns to the same ground, antiquity, desire and grief, and keeps changing shape, so variation is part of the achievement. I share Mattson's admiration for the scale of Cărtărescu's cosmology, and I rank it second. But the stylistic density of the Romanian is carried to me by translation, and I cannot confirm that the achievement I admire is the writer's own prose. For Carson I can judge the language directly. The risk that recurring motifs read as repetition rather than development is also one I find more serious for Cărtărescu's very large scale than for Carson's shifting forms.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and observes that a Carson citation would have to define its scope carefully. The genre labels are contested, and it is uncertain whether the committee would treat the book-object and hybrid works as literature in the sense of Nobel's will.
responses.response: I agree that the scope must be defined with care, and that is why my proposed citation names the renewal of lyric, narrative and the essay, not book-objects as such. I would rest the case on Autobiography of Red and on the written text of Nox, whose elegiac language works on the page even though its physical form adds to it. Contested genre labels seem to me a reason to define the claim precisely, not a reason to set the work aside. I accept his point that later work depending on formal gesture may be harder to judge, and I cannot resolve it from public knowledge alone.

responses.point: Olsson argues that Carson's formal achievement is sustained across genres and rests on deep engagement with Greek and Latin literature. He says the hybrid and visual forms and the translations should be treated as part of the achievement, not as peripheral to it.
responses.response: I agree with the grounding in the classical inheritance, and I agree that the intellectual depth is what separates her work from formal novelty. I would qualify the second point. Treating the translations as part of the achievement does not mean crediting them as original creation. For a single-writer citation I would keep them as context that explains the originals, and I would not claim them as literary achievement in themselves. This is a narrower scope than Olsson suggests, and I think it is easier to defend.

responses.point: Carlberg also ranks Carson first and notes that her translations and classical adaptations could blur the boundary of what is credited as original creation. She also observes that the reputation rests on a few landmark books.
responses.response: I share both cautions and have listed them as my own reservations. I think they point toward a narrower citation, not away from Carson. If the committee cannot agree that the later body of work stands up beside the landmark books, I would then look at Cărtărescu or Robinson, whose cases for sustained quality are differently built.

uncertainties: I have not independently verified the corpus, and my knowledge of Carson's shorter, later and performance works is uneven.
It is unresolved how the committee should weigh her translations and scholarship against her original poetry and prose within one citation.
The effect of Nox depends on its physical form, which public summaries cannot convey.
Whether Carson's hybrid practice is read as a core literary achievement within the framework of Nobel's will remains a matter of judgment.
For Cărtărescu and Adonis, the effects of the original Romanian and Arabic are known to me only through translation and public knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Her documented connections are co-election with David Håkansson, work with Kate Larson, work on Selma Lagerlöf and service with the committee colleagues. None of these ties to a shortlisted writer. Her own literary practice is context, not evidence of preference.
